h1: The 8 Best Leaf Blowers Under $100 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Leaf Blowers Under $100: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 leaf blowers under $100 scored on listed airflow, power source, batteries and handling, from corded SENIX to cordless kits.
summary: The SENIX 12 Amp corded blower is the best leaf blower under $100: 700 CFM of listed airflow and no battery to run flat. LOSART's cordless model lists 650 CFM, and PILENTO bundles two 4.0Ah batteries with a fast charger. The MZK and WOLFMEN sit at 450 CFM, while the BLACK+DECKER at 180 CFM is only for patios and light debris.
intro: Under $100, the leaf blower aisle splits into two camps, and the box does not tell you which you are buying. A corded blower trades a cable for unlimited runtime, while a cordless blower trades runtime for freedom. At this price, cordless models often arrive with two batteries, which sounds generous until you compare the amp-hours with the yard in front of you.

We ranked eight blowers that all fall in the $25 to $50 or $50 to $100 price brackets, and scored them on the Primea framework: listed airflow in CFM, power source and runtime, batteries and charger, then handling and value. Several listings give no airflow figure at all, and we say so rather than guess. Airflow numbers on budget blowers are manufacturer claims, so we weighed them with caution.

products.name: SENIX 12 AMP Corded Electric Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A corded 12 amp handheld with 700 CFM listed. Runs as long as you have an outlet.
products.description:
SENIX drives this blower from a 12 amp motor and lists 700 CFM of airflow in a handheld body, priced in the $25 to $50 bracket. With a cord, there is no battery to charge, and power does not fade as the pack drains.

It ranks first because it lists the highest airflow in the group at the lowest price tier, and corded motors hold full output until you unplug them. The tradeoff is reach: you need an extension cord, and a cord snagging on shrubs gets old quickly on a big lot. Against LOSART's cordless model, it gives up freedom and gains consistency.

A good fit for small yards, decks, driveways and garages near an outlet. Large properties need a battery tool instead.
products.idealFor: Small yards, decks and driveways near an outlet.
products.skipIf: You clear a large property far from power.

products.name: LOSART Leaf Blower Cordless
products.verdict: A cordless blower with 650 CFM listed, the strongest battery-powered claim under $100.
products.description:
LOSART lists 650 CFM from a cordless blower in the $50 to $100 bracket, the highest airflow figure among the battery models here. It is a cordless tool, so there is no cable between you and the work.

It ranks second because the listing says little about the battery, with no capacity or runtime, and airflow claims on budget cordless blowers are best treated as marketing. Against PILENTO, which advertises two 4.0Ah batteries and a fast charger, the LOSART promises more air but less clarity about how long it runs.

The pick for buyers who want the most airflow without a cord and accept some uncertainty. Check the battery details with the seller before buying.
products.skipIf: You need documented battery capacity and runtime.

products.name: PILENTO Cordless Leaf Blower with 2 x 4.0Ah Batteries and Fast Charger
products.verdict: Two 4.0Ah batteries and a fast charger make this a swap-and-go kit for the lowest price tier.
products.description:
PILENTO ships its cordless handheld with two 4.0Ah batteries and a fast charger, in the $25 to $50 bracket. Having a second pack means you can charge one while working with the other, which doubles your effective runtime.

It ranks third because the listing gives no airflow figure, so we cannot compare its power to SENIX or LOSART. What it documents instead is the battery system, and 4.0Ah per pack is a respectable capacity for a handheld. Compared with FAOGO, which also offers two batteries, PILENTO states the amp-hours and costs less.

Best for cordless buyers who care about runtime and value. Check the listing for airflow before assuming it clears wet leaves.
products.idealFor: Cordless buyers who want runtime and spare batteries cheaply.
products.skipIf: You want a published airflow number.

products.name: MZK 20V Cordless Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A 20V cordless blower with 450 CFM listed, at the lowest price tier.
products.description:
MZK sells a 20V cordless blower listing 450 CFM in the $25 to $50 bracket. The 20V platform is a common battery size for budget tools, which can make replacement batteries easier to source.

It ranks fourth because 450 CFM is well below SENIX's 700 and LOSART's 650, so it moves less debris per pass. For dry leaves on a lawn or a driveway that is adequate, but wet piles and heavy debris will test it. Next to WOLFMEN, which lists the same 450 CFM at a higher price bracket, the MZK is the better value.

A sensible pick for light autumn cleanup on a small yard. Plan on short, repeated passes.
cons: Less airflow than the top picks
products.idealFor: Light autumn cleanup on a small yard.
products.skipIf: You face piles of wet leaves.

products.name: WOLFMEN Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A cordless blower listing 450 CFM, matching the MZK at a higher price.
products.description:
WOLFMEN lists 450 CFM from a cordless leaf blower in the $50 to $100 bracket, the same airflow figure as the MZK but costing more.

It ranks fifth because nothing in the listing justifies the extra money over the MZK: there is no battery capacity, no included charger detail and no feature the cheaper model lacks. The airflow is also lower than LOSART's 650 CFM for the same price tier. In its favour, a higher price sometimes means a better warranty or build, though the listing does not say so.

A reasonable choice only if you find it on sale. Otherwise the MZK or LOSART offer a clearer deal.

products.name: FAOGO Cordless Leaf Blower with 2 Batteries & Charger - 990,000 RPM
products.verdict: Two batteries and a charger, but a headline of 990,000 RPM that tells you little.
products.description:
FAOGO bundles a cordless handheld blower with two batteries and a charger, in the $50 to $100 bracket, and leads its title with a 990,000 RPM figure.

It ranks sixth because RPM is not a useful measure of blowing power: airflow in CFM and speed in MPH are what clear leaves, and the listing offers neither. A large motor speed number often says more about marketing than output. Compared with PILENTO, which states 4.0Ah per battery at a lower price tier, FAOGO's battery capacity is unknown.

It will do for light work, but PILENTO documents more. Ask the seller for CFM and amp-hours before buying.
products.idealFor: Light yard work where a spare battery helps.
products.skipIf: You want airflow and runtime documented.

products.name: YOOVL Leaf Blower Cordless
products.verdict: A cordless handheld with almost nothing stated, priced at the low end of the $50 to $100 bracket.
products.description:
YOOVL's cordless blower is a handheld sold in the $50 to $100 bracket, and the listing states little beyond that: no airflow, no battery capacity and no accessories.

It ranks seventh because there is simply less to evaluate. A blower with no stated CFM, voltage or amp-hours forces a purchase on trust, and the better-documented MZK and PILENTO cost less. The cordless format is its one clear benefit, and the lack of a cord keeps it easy to use around garden beds.

Worth considering only if you find it on sale and verify the specs first. Otherwise buy a better documented model.
products.idealFor: Casual users who find it on sale.
products.skipIf: You want to compare numbers before buying.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Electric Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A known-brand handheld at only 180 CFM, suited to patios and light debris.
products.description:
BLACK+DECKER lists 180 CFM from a handheld electric blower in the $25 to $50 bracket, the lowest airflow figure in this guide by a large margin.

It ranks last because 180 CFM is a quarter of the SENIX's 700, which means it takes far more passes to move the same pile. What it offers is the reassurance of a major brand, simple controls and a small footprint, which suit sweeping a patio, a porch or a garage floor more than a lawn. Next to the MZK, it moves less air for a similar price.

A fit for light duty near the house. For a yard of leaves, buy a higher-airflow model.
products.idealFor: Sweeping patios, porches and garage floors.
products.skipIf: You need to clear a lawn of leaves.

whatMatters.detail: Airflow is quoted in cubic feet per minute, written CFM, and it predicts better than any other number how much debris a blower clears in one pass. Higher is better for piles and wet leaves. Budget listings often quote the maximum under ideal conditions, so use CFM to compare blowers, not to promise real-world results.

A corded blower runs at full power for as long as it is plugged in but limits your reach to the cord. A cordless blower is free to move but runs for a limited time and slows as the battery drops. Choose by yard size: small yards favour corded, large yards favour cordless with spare batteries.

Amp-hours (Ah) describe how long a battery lasts, so a 4.0Ah pack runs roughly twice as long as a 2.0Ah pack at the same draw. Two packs let you swap and keep working. Look for amp-hours in the title or specs, because a battery with no stated capacity is a risk.

A 20V platform is a common size, and sharing it with other tools makes spare batteries easier to find. Higher voltage generally means more power. Check whether the listing names a voltage, since cordless blowers without one are harder to compare and to support later, since a battery that fits only one tool is expensive to replace once it fades.

A handheld blower is light enough to carry for 20 or 30 minutes but gets tiring beyond that, and noise can annoy neighbours. Check weight in the listing, wear ear protection for long sessions, and use short bursts. Corded motors tend to be lighter because they carry no battery, which matters when you hold the tool at arm's length for a whole yard.

faq.q: Is a corded leaf blower better than cordless under $100?
faq.a: For power per dollar, yes. The SENIX 12 Amp lists 700 CFM in the lowest price tier and never runs flat. Cordless blowers like the PILENTO trade that for freedom and runtime limits.

faq.q: What mistake do buyers make with budget blowers?
faq.a: Trusting an RPM headline. The FAOGO quotes 990,000 RPM, which says little about how much air actually moves. Look for CFM instead, as the SENIX, LOSART, MZK and WOLFMEN listings provide, and compare those.

faq.q: Is the LOSART worth it over the PILENTO?
faq.a: If airflow matters most, yes. The LOSART lists 650 CFM, while the PILENTO lists none but ships two 4.0Ah batteries and a charger for less. Pick the PILENTO for runtime and the LOSART for power.

faq.q: How do I set up a cordless blower?
faq.a: Charge the batteries fully before first use, attach the nozzle, and test on dry leaves. With the PILENTO, charge the second pack while using the first, so you can swap and keep going.

faq.q: How do I maintain a leaf blower?
faq.a: Keep the intake clear of leaves and dust, and store batteries indoors at moderate temperatures. Corded models like the SENIX need cord inspection, and cordless packs last longer if not left fully drained.

faq.q: Can the BLACK+DECKER handle a lawn full of leaves?
faq.a: Slowly. At 180 CFM it takes many passes where the SENIX at 700 CFM needs fewer. It is better suited to porches, patios and garage floors than to leaf-covered lawns.

finalTake: For most small yards the SENIX 12 Amp corded blower is the right answer: 700 CFM listed and no battery to manage, for the lowest price tier. If you need cordless, buy the LOSART for airflow or the PILENTO for two 4.0Ah batteries. The MZK covers light work cheaply, while the BLACK+DECKER is only for patios.
